title: Paragraphs out of a UN document
problem: Our office copies paragraphs out of UN documents by hand. Can a tool turn a General Comment into a clean list of numbered paragraphs we can cite and reuse, and show me where it may have got things wrong?
facilitator_brief: The file is CESCR General comment No. 27 as OHCHR publishes it in HTML, with a reference (paragraph count, footnote count, first words of each paragraph). The tool must check itself against the reference, say what the HTML version lacks, and let us take the paragraphs away as a dataset, in JSON and Markdown.
notes:
The problem: an office copies paragraphs out of UN documents by hand and wants a tool that turns a General Comment into numbered paragraphs it can cite and reuse, and shows where it may have gone wrong. The facilitator adds three things: check the result against the reference, say plainly what the HTML version lacks, and let the office take the paragraphs away as a dataset, in JSON and Markdown. The data is one document, CESCR General comment No. 27, as the OHCHR treaty body database serves it in HTML, plus a reference: the paragraph count, the footnote count and the first six words of each paragraph. The overview: one record, the `html` string of 71,380 characters, with `title`, `symbol`, `doc_url` and `source`, and a `reference` of 90 paragraphs, 141 footnotes, adopted 26 September 2025. The look tool splits it into 128 block elements. By tag: 91 `

`, 24 `

`, 7 `

` and 6 ``, the cover table; six more `

` sit inside those cells, so the DOM has 97 `

` in all. 90 `

` start with a number, a full stop and then text with no space: "1.A clean, healthy…". None has a space after the stop. The PDF's trap in reverse: there every number stood on its own line; here it is glued to its first word, and a split on "1. " finds nothing. The raw HTML: a cover `` with the symbol broken over a `` ("E" in large type, then "/C.12/GC/27"); then a `
` with the committee's name as a bold `

`, the title as an `

` ending in " *", the heading "I.Introduction", and the paragraphs. The note the asterisk points to is not in the file; nor are footnotes or footnote marks: paragraph 1 ends "chemicals and waste." where the PDF has "waste.2". And spaces are missing inside the text: "andthe" in the title, "levels.Key" and "crises“increase" in the first two paragraphs. Counting the sentence joins: 23 places where a lowercase letter, a full stop and a capital letter touch ("extraction.At", "right.States"). Twelve more where a comma, an opening quote or an en dash touch a letter ("land,wetlands", "crises“increase", "challenges –to"). Then a character a reader does not expect: 8 non-breaking hyphens (U+2011) in "business‑related", "large‑scale", "whistle‑blowers", beside 106 ordinary hyphens; a search typed with the hyphen key misses all eight. I then ran the rules in a short script of my own. Every `

` that starts with one to three digits and a full stop: 90 paragraphs, numbered 1 to 90 without a gap, 42 to 253 words each. The headings are 6 roman-numbered `

` and 24 `

`, 4 lettered and 20 plain ("Right to work (art. 6)"); 8 of the 10 labels are glued ("A.General obligations"), 2 have their space ("D. Obligation"). The first six words of 84 paragraphs match the reference exactly; 6 differ (13, 18, 19, 30, 41, 60): five lost a space inside a word pair ("Giventhe", "Partiesto", "theobligation") and one the spaces in "11 (2) (a)". A rule can restore a space only where the characters prove it was there: a full stop or a comma between letters, a quote or an en dash touching a letter. That is 35 places in 24 paragraphs, and it brings paragraph 18 back into line with the reference; the glued word pairs are invisible to a rule, and the reference sees six words, so what sits deeper in a paragraph stays unknown. Then the typography: 26 en dashes, 20 right single quotes, 5 pairs of curly quotes, 2 non-breaking spaces inside headings; the non-breaking hyphens are written as the entity "‑" in the source. Correct, not damage, but anyone searching the text has to know they are there. So the HTML splits more cleanly than the PDF, with no page breaks, headers, footers or footnote blocks to remove, and loses more: all 141 footnotes, every footnote mark, the cover note, and spaces the PDF kept. The app must make both halves visible. Then the shelf. A search on dataset export and Markdown brought The Turing Way's page on documentation and metadata. Quality assurance: the Analysis Function's page on testing code. Citing UN documents: the Dag Hammarskjöld Library's answer. Accessible tables: the A11Y Project checklist and the Analysis Function's tables page, which the earlier plans follow. The Turing Way page says a dataset should travel with a README in plain text that names its source, its fields and its known limitations; that became the Markdown file's front matter and the "limitations" line in every export. The testing page: good tests tell a story, given this data, having run this code, we expect this output; and every bug found gets a test of its own. Here every damage I found gets a named check. The Library lists what a citation carries: the symbol first, the paragraph as the pinpoint, the URL with the date accessed; the fields are stored apart and formatted on copy, and the form is a question. Trade-offs. The script repairs only what the characters prove and logs each repair; the reference is a yardstick, not the truth, and the app never adjusts its count to match it. No footnote extraction: the HTML has none, and the app says so in red instead of hiding the tile. No model calls; nothing leaves the browser. The plan is short on purpose: four tabs, one question each. The five questions are the office's: headings, the missing spaces, the typography, the export formats, the citation form.

questions.question: What should the app do with the document's section headings, such as "Right to work (art. 6)"?

options.label: Section column
options.description: Each paragraph gets the heading it sits under, in a table column and in the exports; headings never appear inside paragraph text.

fragments.text: One row per paragraph: No. | Section | First line | Check. **Section** is the nearest heading above the paragraph ("Right to work (art. 6)"); the expanded row shows the full path ("IV. … › Right to work (art. 6)"). A closed "Headings found: n" box above the table lists them, so none can hide inside a paragraph.
`paragraph` (its number), `section` and `part` (the nearest heading and the roman-numbered section above it)

options.label: Heading rows
options.description: Headings appear as their own grey rows in the table and as records in the exports, in document order, so the result reads like the document's table of contents.

fragments.text: One row per paragraph or heading, in document order: No. | Kind | First line | Check. Headings are rows of their own, grey, bold and unnumbered, with "heading" in the Kind column for screen readers, so the table reads like the document's table of contents and a reader sees where each heading was found.

`kind` ("paragraph" or "heading", in document order), `paragraph` (the number; null for a heading, whose `citation` and `first_words_match` are null too), and for a heading `label` and `level` (2 or 3)

questions.question: The HTML lost spaces inside the text ("levels.Key", "land,wetlands"). Should the app restore the ones a rule can prove, or only point at them?

options.label: Repair and log
options.description: A space is inserted where the characters prove it was there (after a full stop or comma between letters, around a quote or dash), every insertion is listed, and the text as found is kept beside it.

fragments.text: A table of every missing space the rules found and restored: Paragraph | Before | After | Rule, the count per rule above it (sentence, comma, quote, dash join), the inserted space marked; clicking a row opens the paragraph on tab 02. Under it: "Rules restore a space only where the characters prove it was there. Word pairs such as 'Giventhe' are not touched; the first-words check catches them only in a paragraph's first six words."

- **Repairs.** `text` = `text_raw` with a space inserted after a full stop between a lowercase and a capital letter (`/([a-z])\.([A-Z])/g` → "$1. $2"), after a comma between letters (`/([a-z]),([A-Za-z])/g`), before an opening curly quote touching a letter (`/([a-z])“/g`) and after an en dash touching a letter (`/–([A-Za-z])/g`). Each insertion is logged with the paragraph, the rule and 20 characters each side; nothing else changes.
- **Repairs.** n spaces restored in n paragraphs, counted per rule; every one is listed on tab 03, and `text_raw` still holds the text as found.

options.label: Flag only
options.description: The text stays exactly as OHCHR's HTML has it; the places where a space is probably missing are marked in red and listed, for a reader to check.

fragments.text: A table of every place where a space is probably missing: Paragraph | Where (20 characters each side) | Rule, the count per rule above it (sentence, comma, quote, dash join); nothing is changed, and each place is marked in red in the expanded paragraph on tab 02. Under it: "The text is exactly as OHCHR's HTML has it. Each place listed needs one look by a reader before the paragraph is quoted; word pairs such as 'Giventhe' are not found by any rule."

- **No repairs.** `text` equals `text_raw`. The places where a space is probably missing are found by four patterns, a full stop between a lowercase and a capital letter (`/[a-z]\.[A-Z]/g`), a comma between letters (`/[a-z],[A-Za-z]/g`), an opening curly quote touching a letter (`/[a-z]“/g`) and an en dash touching a letter (`/–[A-Za-z]/g`), and stored as `flags` (paragraph, offset, rule), never applied.
- **Flags.** n places in n paragraphs where a space is probably missing, counted per rule; every one is listed on tab 03 and none is changed.

questions.question: The text uses typographic characters (curly quotes, en dashes, non-breaking hyphens) that a keyboard search misses. Keep them only, or add a plain copy?

options.label: Keep as published
options.description: The text keeps every character as OHCHR published it; the app counts them and warns that a search typed on a keyboard must be normalised first.

fragments.text: A small table: Character | Count | Example, one row each for the en dash, the double quotes, the right single quote, the non-breaking hyphen and the non-breaking space, with the monospace hint "on a keyboard: a hyphen and straight quotes". Under it: "Kept exactly as published, in the table and in every export. A search for 'business-related' typed with the hyphen key will not find 'business‑related': normalise the text before searching it."

- **Characters.** Counted over all paragraph texts: en dash (U+2013), double quotes (U+201C, U+201D), right single quote (U+2019), non-breaking hyphen (U+2011), non-breaking space (U+00A0); `text` keeps them as published.

options.label: Add a plain copy
options.description: Beside the published text, a plain copy with straight quotes, ordinary hyphens and spaces, for searching and matching; a toggle shows it, and the exports carry both.

fragments.text: A small table: Character | Count | Replaced by, one row each for the en dash, the left and right double quotes, the right single quote, the non-breaking hyphen and the non-breaking space. Under it a toggle "Show plain text" (a button with `aria-pressed`) that switches the table on tab 02 and the expanded paragraphs to `text_plain`; the exports carry both `text` and `text_plain`. One sentence: "`text` is exactly as published; `text_plain` has straight quotes, an ordinary hyphen and ordinary spaces, for searching and matching. Quote from `text`."

- **Characters.** Counted over all paragraph texts: en dash (U+2013), left and right double quotes (U+201C, U+201D), right single quote (U+2019), non-breaking hyphen (U+2011), non-breaking space (U+00A0). `text_plain` = `text` with U+201C and U+201D → a straight double quote, U+2019 → an apostrophe, U+2013 and U+2011 → a hyphen, U+00A0 → a space; the replacements per character are the counts shown on tab 03. `text` keeps them as published.

questions.question: Which files should the office be able to download?

options.label: JSON and Markdown
options.description: Two files: JSON for further processing and Markdown for reading and for working with a model; both carry the document's metadata.

fragments.text: Two buttons: **Download JSON** and **Download Markdown**.

options.label: Add CSV
options.description: The same two files plus a CSV for Excel, one row per record with the JSON's fields.

fragments.text: Three buttons: **Download JSON**, **Download Markdown** and **Download CSV**. The CSV has one row per record with the JSON's fields as columns, UTF-8 with a byte-order mark, every field double-quoted with inner quotes doubled, CRLF line ends, so Excel opens it.

questions.question: How should each paragraph be cited in the table and the exports?

options.label: Symbol and paragraph
options.description: The short form used in UN practice: the document symbol, then "para." and the number, as in "E/C.12/GC/27, para. 12".

fragments.text: and a **Copy citation** button that copies "`symbol`, para. n" ("E/C.12/GC/27, para. 12") and shows "Copied" for two seconds; the same string is the `citation` field of every export.
- **Citation** = `symbol` + ", para. " + the paragraph number, with `symbol` read from `WORKSHOP_DATA.html_doc`, never typed in.

options.label: Full reference
options.description: Everything the UN Library recommends: title, symbol, adoption date, paragraph, the UN link and the date you accessed it.

fragments.text: and a **Copy citation** button that copies the full reference, "Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, `title`, `symbol` (adopted `reference.adopted`), para. n, `doc_url` (accessed today's date)", and shows "Copied" for two seconds; the same string is the `citation` field of every export, and the header says which style is applied.

- **Citation** is assembled from fields, never typed in: `title`, `symbol` and `doc_url` from `WORKSHOP_DATA.html_doc`, `reference.adopted`, the paragraph number, and the access date from `new Date()` as day, month name, year. Every export also carries `adopted` and `accessed` as fields of their own.

plan_base:
# Paragraphs out of a UN document: the numbered paragraphs of a General Comment, from its HTML, checked against the reference ## Context The user works in an office that quotes UN documents and copies each paragraph by hand. OHCHR's treaty body database serves the document as HTML, which splits cleanly into paragraphs but has lost things on the way. This app turns `WORKSHOP_DATA.html_doc` into numbered paragraphs with the heading each sits under, compares the result with the document's own reference, says plainly what this HTML version lacks, and lets the office take the paragraphs away as a dataset. The document is `html` (a string: parse it with `new DOMParser().parseFromString(html, 'text/html')`); the yardstick is `reference` (`paragraphs`, `footnotes`, `adopted`, `first_words`); `title`, `symbol`, `doc_url` and `source` describe it; nothing is typed in by hand. ## What I found in the data These numbers are from the file I examined; the app computes its own. - One document, 71,380 characters of HTML; `reference.paragraphs` 90, `reference.footnotes` 141, `reference.first_words` keyed by the paragraph number as a string. - **Elements.** A cover `` (the symbol broken over a ``), then `
`: a bold `

` with the committee's name, the title as an `

` ending in " *", 6 roman-numbered `

`, 24 `

` (4 lettered, 20 plain, "Right to work (art. 6)") and 90 numbered `

`; 97 `

` in all. - **Paragraph numbers are glued to the text**: all 90 read "1.A clean…", none "1. A clean". Heading labels too, in 8 of 10 ("I.Introduction"; "D. Obligation" has its space). - **Spaces are missing inside the text.** 23 sentence joins ("levels.Key"), 8 comma joins ("land,wetlands"), 2 quote joins ("crises“increase"), 2 dash joins ("challenges –to"): 35 places in 24 paragraphs that a rule can prove. And word pairs no rule can see: "Giventhe", "Partiesto", "11(2)(a)". The first-words check catches 6 paragraphs (13, 18, 19, 30, 41, 60), only in their first six words. - **Nothing of the footnotes survives**: no footnote text, no footnote marks (the PDF has "waste.2", this file "waste."), and the title's asterisk points to a note that is not in the file. - **Characters a reader does not expect**: 8 non-breaking hyphens (U+2011, "business‑related") beside 106 ordinary ones; 26 en dashes; 20 right single quotes; 5 pairs of curly quotes; 2 non-breaking spaces inside headings. Correct typography that a search typed on a keyboard misses. - Paragraphs are 42 to 253 words of plain prose. ## The app, tab by tab The arrangement of the workshop's Verbatim finder: header, left rail, four numbered tabs. **Header, always visible.** A monospace label "UN DOCUMENT · HTML", the serif `title`, one line: `symbol` linked to `doc_url` (new tab), "adopted `reference.adopted`", `source`. At the right a green dot "n of m checks pass" or a red dot "n checks failed", then "1 source limit" (the footnotes). **Left rail, always visible.** Headed "DOCUMENT": a card with `symbol` in monospace and the short title. Two big serif numbers: "n paragraphs of `reference.paragraphs`" with a thin bar (red when short or over); "0 footnotes of `reference.footnotes`" in red, "not in this HTML". Then "n of m checks pass", linking to tab 04. Under the header, numbered tabs (`role="tablist"`, arrow keys): `01 RESULT · 02 PARAGRAPHS · 03 LOST & CHANGED · 04 CHECKS & EXPORT`. **01 RESULT. Did the app find everything the document has?** Four tiles, big serif numbers, a "How this is computed" line each: **Paragraphs found: n** beside **the document has `reference.paragraphs`** (green when equal, red with the difference); **First words match: n of `reference.paragraphs`**; **Footnotes: 0 of `reference.footnotes`**, in red, "this HTML version has none; see tab 03"; **Spaces: n** repaired or flagged, linking to tab 03. **02 PARAGRAPHS. What does each paragraph say, and how do I cite it?** {{q1}} First line: the first 120 characters cut at a word with "…"; Check: "OK" or "first words differ" (red). Rows are buttons with `aria-expanded`; click or Enter expands the row in place: the full text, verbatim, never shortened; the reference's six words beside the found six; the places repaired or flagged in this paragraph; {{q5}} **03 LOST & CHANGED. What did the HTML version lose or change?** Three blocks, each with a serif title and a count. **Lost: footnotes.** "The document has `reference.footnotes` footnotes. This HTML has 0: no footnote text, no footnote marks, and the note the title's asterisk points to is missing. To cite a footnote, use the PDF or Word version." **Changed: spaces.** {{q2}} **Changed: characters.** {{q3}} **04 CHECKS & EXPORT. Can I trust this, and can I take it away?** The check panel (next section but one), open, every check on one line. Then **Export**. {{q4}} The JSON file is an array of records, each with `symbol`, {{q1.export}}, `text`, `text_raw`, `first_words_match`, `citation`, `doc_url` and `limitations` ("no footnotes in this HTML version; the document has n"). The Markdown file opens with front matter between `---` lines (`title`, `symbol`, `adopted`, `source_url`, `extracted`: today's date, `paragraphs_found`, `paragraphs_expected`, `footnotes`: the same sentence), then the headings as `##` and `###` lines in document order and each paragraph as its number in bold, then its text. File names: the symbol with slashes replaced by hyphens; a Blob URL, UTF-8. Under the buttons a closed heading "Elements found (n)" (a button with `aria-expanded`): every block element in order, Tag | Classified as | Text (first 80 characters). At most seven things to click. **Footer, always visible.** `source`, `built`, and "Done by this page's code; no model was called and nothing left the browser." ## How every number is computed The pipeline runs once on load, over the parsed document's `body` elements in order. - **Classification.** Elements inside the first `

` are cover. After it, a `

` whose text matches `/^(\d{1,3})\.\s*(.*)$/s` is a paragraph with that number; the first `

` is the title; every other `

` and `

` is a heading, split by `/^([IVX]+|[A-Z])\.\s*(.+)$/` into `label` and `heading` when it matches; any other `

` is the committee line. - **Paragraph text.** `text_raw` = the text after the number and full stop, trimmed, runs of whitespace collapsed to one space. {{q2.compute}} {{q3.compute}} - **Section** = the nearest heading above the paragraph; `part` = the nearest roman-numbered `

`. A heading is never paragraph text. - **First words.** The first six whitespace-separated words of `text` against `reference.first_words[String(number)]`: equal after turning curly quotes straight, en dashes and non-breaking hyphens into a hyphen and non-breaking spaces into spaces; case is kept. {{q5.compute}} - **Counts** are loops in JavaScript; nothing is estimated, no model is called. ## How the app checks itself One line per check: what was compared, the two values, and "pass" in green, "check failed" in red with a link to the rows concerned, or "source limit" in red for what the source cannot give. A failed check never hides a result. - **Paragraph count.** Found against `reference.paragraphs`. - **Numbering.** Exactly 1 to n in order; gaps and duplicates listed. - **First words.** Mismatches counted and listed, "para. n: found … / reference …", the row flagged on tab 02. - **Footnotes.** 0 against `reference.footnotes`: "source limit", with "the HTML version has no footnotes: a limit of the source, not of the app", counted apart from failures. {{q2.checks}} - **Headings.** How many `

` and `

`, and how many glued labels were separated. - **Nothing lost.** Every block element is classified exactly once and the counts per class sum to the total; any unclassified element is listed in red. - **Export round trip.** The JSON to download is parsed back; its record count equals the table's. ## Edge cases and risks - A number glued to its text and one followed by a space are both accepted (`\s*`): this file has 90 of the first, none of the second; another file may be the reverse. - A rule may insert a space only where the characters prove one was there. "Giventhe" stays, caught only when it falls in a paragraph's first six words; a reader who quotes a paragraph still reads it. - The reference is a yardstick, not the truth: when the counts disagree, the app shows both and never trims or pads its result to match. - If `reference` or one of its fields is missing, the tiles say "no reference in this file" and the checks that need it show "not run", never "pass"; if `html` yields no `

`, tab 01 says so and the exports are disabled. ## Design and accessibility What this app adds to the studio look: - **Red accent** on the active tab, the paragraph numbers, the footnotes tile and the words "first words differ", "check failed" and "source limit"; "pass" dark green: words as well as colours. - **Big serif numbers** only on the rail and the tiles of tab 01. Every table has a serif `

` stating the message ("90 paragraphs found, 90 expected"), a monospace number (`TAB.01`), `
`, numbers right-aligned. - A repaired or flagged place is marked in the expanded paragraph by a thin red box. - The check panel follows "Quality assurance of code for analysis and research: Testing code" (Analysis Function): each check tells a story, given this data, having run this code, we expect this output; every damage found has a named check. - The exports follow The Turing Way's "Documentation and metadata": a dataset travels with its source, its fields and its known limitations. - Citations follow the Dag Hammarskjöld Library's "How should I cite a UN document?": fields stored apart and formatted on copy, the symbol as the key, the paragraph as the pinpoint. - Keyboard: rows and closed headings are buttons with `aria-expanded`; a hidden tab panel is not focusable. ## Out of scope No footnote extraction: the source has none. No model calls, no summaries, no comparison with the PDF text, no editing in the browser, one document. ## Sources consulted - The Turing Way, Documentation and metadata — https://github.com/the-turing-way/the-turing-way/blob/bcd8050eed319acc55f8ce0fe0410db157a17f04/book/website/reproducible-research/rdm/rdm-metadata.md - UK Government Analysis Function, Quality assurance of code for analysis and research: Testing code — https://github.com/best-practice-and-impact/qa-of-code-guidance/blob/fa39f2089905fe07c08ae4d66671736a1becd3c5/book/testing_code.md - Dag Hammarskjöld Library, Ask DAG: how should I cite a UN document? — https://ask.un.org/faq/401380
